A.explanation: A balance point S must lie between Q and R, so the p.d. across QS cannot exceed the p.d. across QR driven by E. Hence $E_X < E$ is necessary.

B.explanation: At the null point the galvanometer reads zero, so there is no current in the cell X branch and no lost volts across its internal resistance.

C.explanation: The result uses $E_X = E \times QS/QR$, so the balance length QS and total length QR must be measured accurately.

D.explanation: The wire QR must be uniform so p.d. is proportional to length, allowing length ratio to replace voltage ratio.

hints: Look at the movable contact S on wire QR and the galvanometer in series with cell X - the measurement is made when the galvanometer current is zero.
When galvanometer current is zero, there is no current in the cell X loop, so compare the terminal p.d. of X with its e.m.f.
The balance condition gives $E_X/E = QS/QR$, so think about what must be true for S to lie on QR and for length to stand for voltage.
walkthrough: Identify the two loops: cell E drives a steady current through the uniform wire QR, producing a uniform potential drop from Q to R.
Slide contact S until the galvanometer in the lower loop with cell X shows zero deflection. This is the null point where the p.d. across QS opposes and equals $E_X$.
At null there is zero current in the X-galvanometer-S-Q branch, so for cell X, $V = E_X - Ir = E_X - 0 = E_X$. Internal resistance causes no voltage drop.
Because the wire is uniform, $V_{QS}/V_{QR} = QS/QR$. But $V_{QR}$ is set by E and $V_{QS} = E_X$, so $E_X = E \times QS/QR$.
This formula requires S to fall on the wire, so $E_X$ must be less than E, requires accurate $QS$ and $QR$, and requires resistance proportional to length for a uniform gradient.
Knowing the internal resistance of X is never used in the null condition or the ratio, so it is not required. This is option B.
